interactions.label: In a child presenting in coma, the clinician should complete the full assessment

params.question: In a child presenting in coma, the clinician should complete the full assessment before initiating any treatment.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: In paediatric coma, assessment and treatment happen concurrently, not sequentially. The three most common reversible causes — hypoglycaemia, CNS infections, and status epilepticus — can worsen rapidly, so first-line treatments must be started before the full assessment is complete.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. An unconscious child must be assessed and treated simultaneously because the three most common reversible causes — hypoglycaemia, CNS infections, and status epilepticus — can each cause irreversible damage if treatment is delayed while completing assessment.

interactions.label: A 2-year-old in the emergency department has a heart rate of 180/min, cold extre

params.question: A 2-year-old in the emergency department has a heart rate of 180/min, cold extremities, and a capillary refill time of 4 seconds. Blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, which is normal for age. What is the most accurate assessment?

answers.text: The child is not in shock because the blood pressure is normal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blood pressure can remain normal in compensated shock. Children maintain BP by raising heart rate and constricting peripheral vessels, even after 25–30% of blood volume is lost.

answers.text: The child is in compensated shock — tachycardia and poor perfusion indicate inadequate tissue perfusion despite normal blood pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, and cold extremities signal compensated shock. Blood pressure is maintained by compensatory mechanisms and drops only when compensation fails.

answers.text: The child has decompensated shock because the heart rate is elevated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Decompensated shock is defined by the failure of compensatory mechanisms, with falling blood pressure and declining mental status — not by tachycardia alone, which is already present in compensated shock.

answers.text: The child is in irreversible shock and aggressive treatment is unlikely to help

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Irreversible shock implies established organ damage unresponsive to treatment. This child's preserved blood pressure indicates compensation is still active, making this the ideal window for intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: in children, shock is diagnosed by tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cold extremities, and altered mental status — not by blood pressure, which drops only when compensation fails.
Well done. Compensated shock is diagnosed by clinical signs of poor perfusion — not by blood pressure, which is a late marker.

interactions.label: A 4-year-old has been having continuous generalised tonic-clonic seizures for 7

params.question: A 4-year-old has been having continuous generalised tonic-clonic seizures for 7 minutes. The nurse suggests continuing observation until 30 minutes before treating. Based on the ILAE definition of status epilepticus, what is the correct response?

answers.text: The nurse is correct — treatment for status epilepticus begins only after 30 minutes of continuous seizure activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 30-minute threshold (t2) marks the point at which lasting brain injury becomes likely. Treatment must start much earlier, at t1 = 5 minutes.

answers.text: The 30-minute threshold applies to adults only; the paediatric threshold is 15 minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The t1 threshold of 5 minutes applies to convulsive status epilepticus in both adults and children. There is no separate 15-minute threshold in the ILAE framework.

answers.text: Treatment timing depends entirely on the seizure type and should await EEG confirmation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Convulsive status epilepticus is a clinical diagnosis. Waiting for EEG confirmation delays life-saving benzodiazepine administration and worsens outcomes.

answers.text: Treatment should have started at 5 minutes — seizures beyond this point rarely self-terminate, and each additional minute reduces benzodiazepine efficacy due to receptor internalisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The ILAE defines t1 as 5 minutes for generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Benzodiazepine receptors undergo internalisation during prolonged seizures, making delayed treatment progressively less effective.

overallFeedback.feedback: The ILAE defines two timepoints: t1 (5 minutes) for treatment initiation and t2 (30 minutes) for risk of lasting brain injury. Benzodiazepines must be given at t1, because their efficacy drops with each passing minute due to receptor internalisation.
Correct. Treat at 5 minutes — the old 30-minute threshold has been abandoned because delayed treatment allows receptor downregulation and worsens prognosis.

interactions.label: During single-rescuer CPR on an 8-month-old infant, which compression technique

params.question: During single-rescuer CPR on an 8-month-old infant, which compression technique and compression-to-ventilation ratio should be used?

answers.text: Heel of one hand on the lower sternum, 30 compressions to 2 breaths

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The heel-of-hand technique is used for children aged 1 year to puberty, not for infants under one year.

answers.text: Two thumbs encircling the chest, 15 compressions to 2 breaths

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The two-thumb encircling technique is used only with two rescuers in infants, with a 15:2 ratio. A single rescuer uses the two-finger technique with a 30:2 ratio.

answers.text: Two fingers on the centre of the chest just below the nipple line, 30 compressions to 2 breaths

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. For single-rescuer infant CPR, two fingers are placed over the centre of the chest just below the nipple line, compressing to about 4 cm depth at 100–120/min, with a 30:2 ratio.

answers.text: Two hands on the lower sternum, 15 compressions to 2 breaths

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Two-hand compressions are reserved for larger children approaching puberty. For infants, a single rescuer uses the two-finger technique with a 30:2 ratio.

overallFeedback.feedback: For single-rescuer infant CPR: two fingers on the centre of the chest just below the nipple line, compress ~4 cm deep at 100–120/min, 30 compressions then 2 breaths. With two rescuers, switch to two thumbs encircling the chest with a 15:2 ratio.
Well done. Single-rescuer infant CPR uses two fingers just below the nipple line, compressing to ~4 cm at 100–120/min with a 30:2 ratio.

interactions.label: A child on a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min shows a pulse oximetry reading of 9

params.question: A child on a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min shows a pulse oximetry reading of 97%. The resident concludes the child is improving. Which limitation of pulse oximetry makes this conclusion potentially unsafe?

answers.text: Pulse oximetry does not measure carbon dioxide — the child may be retaining CO₂ with rising hypercapnia despite adequate SpO₂

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation only. On supplemental oxygen, SpO₂ can remain high even as CO₂ accumulates, masking respiratory failure. Clinical signs — respiratory rate, effort, alertness — must always be assessed alongside.

answers.text: Pulse oximetry is unreliable in all children under 5 years of age

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pulse oximetry is reliable across all paediatric ages. Its limitations relate to perfusion state and what it measures — not to the patient's age.

answers.text: A reading of 97% always indicates the child needs less supplemental oxygen, confirming improvement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A high SpO₂ on supplemental oxygen shows adequate oxygenation at that moment but says nothing about ventilation or the trajectory of the child's work of breathing. It does not confirm improvement.

answers.text: The non-rebreather mask interferes with the pulse oximetry probe and produces falsely high readings

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The oxygen delivery device does not affect the probe. Falsely abnormal readings occur with poor perfusion, hypothermia, or motion artefact — not with the type of mask used.

overallFeedback.feedback: Pulse oximetry does not measure CO₂. On supplemental oxygen, a normal SpO₂ can mask worsening ventilation. The clinician must combine oximetry with clinical signs — respiratory rate, retractions, alertness, and colour — to judge whether the child is truly improving.
Correct. SpO₂ can look falsely reassuring on supplemental oxygen while CO₂ quietly rises. Always assess respiratory rate, effort, consciousness, and skin colour alongside the oximetry reading.
